messages:
alice: Quick sync — hitting a weird pattern in the Python SSE client when under steady high QPS. We get a burst of partial JSON objects (split across chunks) and the read loop backs up, leading to a slow-consumer backlog. Anyone tried an "adaptive drain" strategy?

kai: I saw something similar last month. Can you paste a tiny repro or the read loop?

alice: gist: short pseudocode below — basically the asyncio reader pushes bytes to a queue and a parser coroutine tries to decode NDJSON entries.

alice: ```python
async def reader(ws, q):
    while True:
        chunk = await ws.read(4096)  # can be smaller in practice
        await q.put(chunk)

async def parser(q):
    buf = b""
    while True:
        chunk = await q.get()
        buf += chunk
        try:
            while b"\n" in buf:
                line, buf = buf.split(b"\n", 1)
                obj = json.loads(line)
                handle(obj)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            # wait for more bytes
            pass
```

alice: Under load, q grows and parser can't keep up because json.loads is expensive on big partial buffers.

marc: Two quick ideas: 1) limit q maxsize and have reader await q.put (backpressure). 2) use incremental JSON parser (like ijson) to avoid concatenating huge buffers.

sam: +1 to queue sizing. We did maxsize=1000 for a different service and used a small sleep in reader when queue is above threshold — basically cooperative backpressure to avoid OOM.

nish: If you have many tiny chunks (utf8 multibyte splits) the naive split-by-newline can still leave you with big buf because the parser stalls on a long unfinished object. Consider emitting partial frames to a worker pool for parsing small batches.

alice: Thoughts on adaptive drain: reader measures q.qsize() and avg chunk size. If qsize > high_watermark: switch parser to "fast mode" where it attempts to parse small prefix-only (try-except per line) and any remaining buf gets trimmed to a safety window (e.g., keep last 16KB). Also apply gzip-level heuristics?

kai: fast-mode sounds risky if you drop bytes. Instead consider these non-destructive tactics: - prefix/KV cache reuse to reduce parse cost - parsing in threads via run_in_executor to avoid blocking event loop - slice the buffer into smaller JSON candidates and submit each to a worker pool (bounded)

marc: We've used an approach where parser keeps a rolling deque of bytes and only gives workers complete-line slices. If a worker is slow, you can increase worker count or reduce per-worker batch size. Crucial: don't let reader keep appending to a single monolithic bytes object; use list of chunks and only join when you have a complete line.

alice: Example change I pushed locally: store chunks in a deque, only join up to first newline. Cut off pre-newline join length to 64KB and if exceeded, drop with a metric + warn. People hate dropping, but it kept the service stable.

sam: Also consider using asyncio.Queue.get_nowait in a loop to batch read multiple chunks per iteration into parser, then process them as a batch — reduces context switches.

nish: For auth-related retries: ensure token refresh doesn't block the reader. We saw tokens renewing inside the read task and that stalls everything. Put refresh in a separate coroutine and have reader check current token validity on reconnect only.

alice: Good call — our client was reauthing inline when a 401 arrived mid-stream. Moved that logic to reconnect handler.

deploy-bot: deploy: staging updated with alice/sse-adaptive-drain (2026-03-18T14:05:12Z) :rocket:

kai: One more: instrument per-message latency and queue depth, emit alerts when parsing lag > X ms. That gives a signal before consumer collapses.

marc: If you're using CPython, json library is C-optimized but still CPU-bound. Offload to a process pool if you expect bursts.

alice: Thanks — plan: 1) implement bounded queue + reader await, 2) switch to chunk-deque + join-on-newline, 3) offload parsing to thread/process pool, 4) add metrics + alert. Will ping when I have a minimal repro for the devex SDK tests.

sam: Happy to review the PR. Also test with artificially split multibyte sequences (emojis) — they love to break naive UTF-8 slicing.

nish: If you want, I can share our ijson-based snippet that streams into objects without full-line reliance.

alice: That'd be great, thanks! :heart:

kai: Thanks for the writeup. Small nit: include the websocket client version and whether you're using httpx or aiohttp — they differ in backpressure characteristics.

alice: Using aiohttp 3.9.4. Will add that to the repro.

sam: 👍

alice: I'll update the thread with the PR link and a tiny repro script later today. Appreciate the pointers.
